items.title: Jimmy Owens — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Side bar—1968, working with Duke Ellington, I was doing a movie score with him called “Change of Mind”... I came down to the saxophone section, sat in Procope’s seat and played the alto saxophone part on flugelhorn.

ctx.x: When you were a child, did you hear jazz in the house?

Oh yes, my father played jazz all the time on the record player, Victrola. When I was three or four years old, I had my favorite records that I could go and pick out the record and put it on the Victrola and play it. The music that my father played most of the time were people like Duke Ellington, Billie Holliday, Count Basie’s band, Charlie Shavers, this is what I was hearing when I was a kid.
Do you remember the first live jazz that you heard?

items.title: Jimmy Owens interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: working with Duke Ellington and Count Basie. All of that has been a very important part of my performing career.

ctx.x: The association of jazz with drugs and so forth is pretty documented. Has it changed over the years? Has it gotten better or worse?

Oh most definitely. It’s gotten better because life in America has gotten better. As we pinpointed racism a little more and made things better for African American people, narcotics stopped a little bit in the jazz musician — a lot I should say — in the jazz musician community. It’s really difficult being in Duke Ellington’s band and traveling through the south in the 30s. There were no hotels. Being Billie Holiday, being Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong. There were no hotels, there were no places to eat. I mean…
Do you think there’s a misdirected opinion with some of the European musicians that the narcotics help you to play this?
